text:
I felt my jaw tighten. I didn't look at him, instead focusing on a deep scratch on the wooden surface of the desk. My fingers curled into a fist, the fabric of my hoodie bunching up. The same stupid questions, the same assumption that my life is some kind of open book for everyone to flip through.

"I said Tver. I don't know who the hell you think I am, but I'm not from St. Pete," I spat, my voice sounding sharper than I intended. I finally turned my head to glare at him, my eyes narrow. "And Marinka needs to shut her mouth before she starts making things up about people who actually matter. I don't play. I don't 'do' class parties. So just sit there and be quiet, or go find someone else to annoy."

"I said Tver, not St. Petersburg. Are you even listening or just waiting for your turn to talk?" I snapped, my voice sounding harsher than I intended. I reached for my headphones, pulling them over my ears to block out the world, though I didn't turn on any music. "And Marinka needs to shut her mouth. I don't play anymore. I don't care about your party, and I definitely don't care about 'blowing anyone away.' Just drop it."

text:
I felt the blood rush to my face, and my grip tightened on the edge of the desk until my knuckles turned white. The mention of the violin hit me like a physical blow, making the air in the room feel suddenly thin. I shoved my chair back with a loud, grating screech that echoed through the nearly empty classroom.

"I'm from Tver, not St. Pete. Can you even listen?" I snapped, my voice coming out sharper than I intended. I reached for my headphones and yanked them over my ears, effectively cutting off the world. "And Marinka needs to keep her mouth shut about things she doesn't know. I don't play anymore. Period."

I didn't look at him. I couldn't. I just stared at the grey drizzle outside the window, my chest heaving slightly. The thought of touching that instrument again made my stomach churn. I just wanted him to leave before I said something I couldn't take back.

text:
I paused, my hand still resting on the counter, and let my gaze drift from the rain-streaked window back to you. A slow smile tugged at the corner of my mouth. The invitation was bold, but there was something about the way you said it—almost as if you'd been rehearsing it in your head while waiting for your coffee.

— Vinyl, huh? — I let out a soft, ironic huff, sliding the empty cup away. — You're trying to tempt me with the classics. I'm a sucker for a good record, and frankly, my thesis is currently staring at me from my laptop with a look of utter disappointment. I could use a distraction.

I reached over and clicked the lock on the front door, pulling the keys from the wall with a metallic jingle. I stepped around the counter, the smell of cinnamon following me as I stopped just a few inches from you.

— But let's get one thing straight: if Pumpkin decides your sofa is a scratching post, you're the one who has to explain it to me. — I tilted my head, my green eyes scanning your face. — Lead the way, neighbor. I'm curious to see if your taste in music is as good as your timing.

text:
I paused, my fingers tracing the rim of the empty espresso cup. The invitation was bold, and the irony of it—being invited to a place where I'd actually be *heard* instead of just serving coffee—wasn't lost on me. I looked at the clock again, then back at you, a slow smile spreading across my lips.

— Bold of you to assume I don't have a better bed than a cafe bench, — I said, my voice dropping an octave. I reached over and grabbed my keys, the metal jingling against the counter. — But vinyl and wine? That's a hard offer to turn down. Especially since I've been staring at the back of your head for a month and wondering if you're as interesting as your coffee order suggests.

I stepped around the counter, the scent of cinnamon following me as I closed the distance. I stopped just close enough for you to see the green of my eyes.

— I'll go grab Pumpkin first. If you can handle a cat that thinks it owns the world, I might just take you up on that. Give me fifteen minutes to get the little tyrant, and I'll be at your door. Don't drink all the wine before I get there.

text:
I paused, my fingers drumming slowly on the polished wood of the counter. The invitation was bold, but the way you said it—as if it were the most logical solution to the weather—made me smile. I looked at the door, then back at you, letting the silence stretch just long enough to make you wonder if you'd pushed too far.

"You've got a lot of confidence for someone who hasn't even asked for my number yet," I said, my voice dropping an octave. I reached for my bag, pulling out my keys and sliding them into my pocket. "But I'm a sucker for vinyl. And Pumpkin is a very judgmental cat; he'll let me know immediately if your place is up to his standards."

I stepped around the counter, the scent of cinnamon following me as I approached. I stopped just close enough that you could see the green of my eyes. "But if the wine is cheap, I'm leaving through the window."
